kp.k: Both first-year and lateral hiring contracted in 2023
kp.d: Leopard Solutions challenges the Thomson Reuters Institute LFFI account that the hiring slowdown was localized to new associates while lateral hiring remained brisk. Its January–September counts show first-year hires declining from 4,432 in 2021 and 3,684 in 2022 to 2,591 in 2023; lateral hires declined from 7,860 and 7,983 to 5,264. The document addresses legal employment trends without attributing these changes to AI.
qs: Yes, hiring first-years is indeed on a downswing, but the numbers tell us so, too, is lateral hiring.

kp.k: Leopard interprets contraction as a post-pandemic market correction
kp.d: The article interprets the 2023 decline against two years of unusually strong hiring, rather than as a wholesale strategic pivot. It links the cooling of hiring to layoffs following the post-pandemic hiring surge. This is Leopard's explanation of the pattern, distinct from the reported hiring counts.
qs: As depicted in the chart above, the decreases come after two years of unrestrained hiring. and when analyzed over time, it should be perceived as a market correction rather than a wholesale strategic pivot.
Some firms laid off in droves following the post-pandemic splurge, leading all hiring to cool.

kp.k: Leopard reports steeper declines than the LFFI
kp.d: For Am Law 100 first-year hiring, Leopard reports a 36% decline in 2023 against the 2021/2022 average of 4,058, compared with the LFFI's reported 17% decline. It also reports a 34% lateral-hiring decline for the same demographic against an average of 7,921. For Am Law 200 first-year class sizes, Leopard reports a 28% decline, compared with the LFFI's 25%. These are the article's stated comparisons, not independently reconciled measures.
qs: the LFFI average number of new first-year associates at Am Law 100 firms was down 17% this past September as compared with the average from the previous two years.
Leopard Solutions calculated the same metric at 36%, more than double that percentage (Average of 2021/2022 new hires 4,058/2023 New = 2591).
Similarly, we also found a decrease in lateral hiring for the same demographic which was 34% (7921/2023 LAT = 5264).
The LFFI listed first-year class sizes as having fallen in size by an average of 25% among the Am Law 200 firms, whereas our percentage was slightly higher at 28%.

kp.k: Longer-term hiring preferences shifted toward lateral associates
kp.d: Alongside its cyclical explanation of the 2023 contraction, Leopard identifies a longer-term shift away from entry-level recruitment toward laterals. It states that Big Law once hired twice as many graduates as laterals, but that the pattern reversed in 2018, when only 55 firms in the referenced group hired more entry-level than lateral associates.
qs: It is evident that the decline in entry-level hiring has been occurring over the years in favor of a shift to hiring laterals.
Big Law once hired twice as many law graduates as laterals, but in 2018, that paradigm flipped.
only 55 firms in this group hired more entry-level associates than lateral associates.

kp.k: Higher lateral salaries may explain rising direct expenses
kp.d: Leopard proposes that increasingly expensive lateral recruitment may help explain the more than 6% rise in overall law firm direct expenses in the third quarter of 2023 reported by Reuters. It presents this as a possible explanation beyond headcount growth alone, not as an established causal finding.
qs: This trend of championing a lateral market that commands higher and higher salaries may also be the reason Reuters reported overall law firm direct expenses were up more than 6% in the third quarter of 2023, as opposed to solely attributing the expenses to the increase to headcount growth.

kp.k: Lateral dependence risks long-term associate development
kp.d: The article argues that recruiting successful attorneys offers transferable business and proven high-fee earners, but warns that firms cannot depend indefinitely on lateral hiring. It raises responsibility for training new associates and asserts that firms are promoting entry-level hires at a lower level than previously, without quantifying that claim; it suggests smaller entry-level cohorts may explain part, but not all, of the change.
qs: The calculus is simple: recruiting already successful attorneys brings with it transferable business, proven high-fee earners, and an established book of business.
Lateral hiring may scratch an itch; however, this new hiring strategy puts firms at risk down the road.
Firms must contend with the question of who will train new associates. In the long term, they cannot depend on lateral hiring alone.
They are also promoting entry-level hires are a lower level than in the past. It could be due to their fewer numbers but not totally.

kp.k: Hiring evidence comes from an unaudited proprietary tracker
kp.d: The supplied document specifies that the counts cover January–September hires within Leopard's tracked firm population. Its concluding contextual note identifies firm websites and announcements as the underlying monitoring sources and states that the article has no methodology section or author byline and that the counts are not audited.
qs: Counts are January-September year-to-date hires into the firm population Leopard tracks (the article's chart, reproduced as text in the body above).
The article carries no author byline and no methodology section; the underlying tracker is Leopard's firm-website and announcement monitoring, and the counts are Leopard's, not audited.

pts.k: The source makes no claims or predictions about AI changing legal services, employment, or legal markets.
pts.d: Leopard Solutions attributes the 2023 hiring contraction to a correction following post-pandemic hiring and discusses a longer-term preference for lateral recruitment. It does not mention AI or connect hiring declines, recruitment strategy, or associate training risks to AI. This is a legal-sector source, not a cross-domain source; its non-AI hiring claims therefore do not constitute claims within the requested category.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No evidence is offered concerning AI's effects.
pts.d: The source offers proprietary first-year and lateral hiring counts for January–September 2021, 2022, and 2023, and comparisons with Thomson Reuters Institute figures. These support its discussion of hiring trends, not an AI-related explanation. No AI adoption measures, AI benchmarks, or evidence connecting AI to employment changes are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI-related timeframe or conditions are stated.
pts.d: The hiring comparisons concern January–September 2023 relative to 2021 and 2022. The source also discusses a recruitment shift evident in 2018 and unspecified long-term risks from relying on lateral hiring. None of these timeframes is attached to an AI claim.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No group is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The non-AI discussion concerns law firms, including Am Law 100 and Am Law 200 firms, first-year associates, lateral attorneys, and the future training of new associates. The source does not describe AI-driven effects on any of these groups.
